items.title: A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It's Addictive
items.summary:
A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It’s Addictive

Unlike the pillowy-soft focaccia that’s more
items.text:
A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It’s Addictive

Unlike the pillowy-soft focaccia that’s more widely known, focaccia di Recco is thin, crispy and filled with gooey cheese

This summer, I found myself on a mission. As temperatures soared into the mid-90s during Europe’s heat wave, I packed my bags and embarked on a six-hour road trip from Switzerland to Liguria. Rather than seeking out seasonal treats like granita or gelato, I was headed to the Italian coast for focaccia.

When most Americans­—and Italians, for that matter—think of focaccia, they think of the pillowy-soft version that’s leavened with yeast, baked in a sheet pan and perfect for scarpetta, or the mopping up of delicious sauces. However, ask any Ligurian, and they will tell you that the focaccia that reigns supreme is focaccia di Recco.

Focaccia di Recco is a specialty dish in Liguria. Starkly different from the carbohydrate found in the United States, this yeast-free snack is a thin flatbread filled with gooey cheese—usually crescenza or stracchino—and baked in a super-hot oven until crispy and golden brown.

Certified as just one of four foods of the Ligurian coast with a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation from the European Union, an official focaccia di Recco can be made only in Recco or neighboring Camogli, Sori or Avegno. Along with sea-salt cured anchovies, basil and olive oil, focaccia di Recco is the pride of the Ligurian people. For two decades, a consortium, the Consorzio della Focaccia di Recco, has safeguarded the legend of the bread by promoting it through annual events like the Recco Focaccia Festival.

“The focaccia di Recco celebrates authenticity, local traditions and is a connection between food, people and place,” says Giovanni Astolfoni, a Genoa native who is executive chef of Botanico Restaurant in Nervi. “It is much more than a local specialty. It perfectly reflects the spirit of Ligurian cooking. … It looks simple, yet making it well takes experience, patience and respect for the ingredients.”

Even revered pizza makers in Italy hold focaccia di Recco in high esteem, agreeing that it is worth the pilgrimage. “What impresses me most is its simplicity and the incredible craftsmanship behind it,” says Francesco Capece, owner of Confine in Milan, recently named Italy’s best pizzeria. “With just a few ingredients, it creates a perfect balance between the crispy, paper-thin dough and the creamy cheese filling. It is a beautiful example of how Italian tradition transforms simple ingredients into something extraordinary.”

History of Focaccia di Recco

According to the consortium, the history of focaccia di Recco can be traced back to 1189, when a version of the bread appeared on the table of medieval knights before they made their departure for the Holy Land during the Third Crusade. However, it was during the raids by Saracen pirates around the 16th century that focaccia di Recco became what it is today, confirms Lucio Bernini, the consortium’s director. Research shows that as locals from Recco fled to the mountains, the ingredients they carried with them—flour, oil and cheese—were combined and cooked over slate stone. At the end of the 1800s, bakeries and taverns sold focaccia di Recco to residents in celebration of All Souls’ Day (November 2), the day after All Saints’ Day, which marks a two-day Christian observance of saints and martyrs, as well as those who are deceased. Nowadays, focaccia di Recco is a staple in the Ligurian diet, with locals in the region’s four provinces having constant access to it throughout the day.

Did you know? The earliest focaccia

Neolithic communities in the Middle East were baking focaccia-like flatbreads between 7000 and 5000 B.C.E., according a 2024 study in Scientific Reports.

In the 19th century, Panificio Moltedo, a bakery that still stands in Recco, was the first to sell focaccia di Recco. The now fifth-generation-owned bakery recently celebrated its 150th year making its wafer-thin pastry; unlike other bakeries and taverns, Panificio Moltedo does not bake its focaccia in a pan but rather directly on the deck of the oven, like a pizza, for maximum crispness. Another longtime favorite is Manuelina. The restaurant’s namesake ran a tavern outside of Recco in the late 1800s and is credited with making focaccia di Recco mainstream by serving it every day. Her descendants opened a simple focacceria in town in 1983 to keep up with demand. “Manuelina took the popular recipe and was the first to start selling it every day and for everyone to enjoy, But they did not invent focaccia di Recco,” says Bernini.

In the past century and a half, a handful of other eateries have opened along the Italian Riviera selling focaccia di Recco. One of those is Revello Camogli in the resort town of Camogli. “We have been making focaccia di Recco ever since my grandfather took over the business in 1964,” says third-generation owner Umberto Revello. “Running a bakery like ours requires a great deal of time, so the bakery becomes a second home—if not the first. Since we were children, we have grown up watching our father and grandfather make focaccia every day. It naturally became part of our family tradition.” He says that it’s more than a family business; focaccia represents an important part of his identity.

Second-generation focaccia di Recco maker Fabrizio Passano agrees. “My father, Alfredo, started making focaccia di Recco in 1967, and for the last 59 years, we have continued the tradition,” says the chef at Alfredo Ristorante in Recco. “Focaccia di Recco is a symbol of an ancient tradition we hold incredibly dear.”

Once I arrived in Recco, the focaccia, advertised on blackboard menus and in bakeries around town, was hard to miss. The blisters that formed on the roof of my mouth as I sampled different vendors’ versions of the bread filled with piping hot cheese were well worth it.

“While every restaurant has their own differences in technique, there really is only one recipe,” says Passano, acknowledging the focaccia’s PGI status. “So you have to stick with the plan.” When I stop into Alfredo Ristorante, the chef tosses the focaccia dough in the air with very little effort. Clearly, he has made many, and the result is a very thin and crispy focaccia. The cheese is chewy and makes a squeaking noise when I bite into it.

Over lunch at Alfredo, Bernini tells me the consortium consists of 12 members with 19 destinations, including bakeries, take-away eateries and restaurants spread across the Ligurian coast. “The PGI preserves the true history and tradition against increasingly widespread imitations,” the former hotelier adds.

According to Bernini, without the PGI stamp, the focaccia should not be called focaccia di Recco and should bear the name focaccia col formaggio (focaccia with cheese). A handful of restaurants in the United States, including Chi Spacca in Los Angeles, Rosie Cannonball in Houston and Keste in New York City, have the specialty on their menus.

How to make focaccia di Recco

According to Bernini, Passano and Revello, achieving a perfect focaccia di Recco comes down to the skills of the focacciai (a Ligurian term for focaccia makers). But all three agree that you can make the bread at home with a few simple tips.

“An important element to making a great focaccia di Recco is using high-quality ingredients,” says Revello. He continues, “Firstly, the flour. We use a strong Italian Type ‘0’ flour, which has an appearance of traditional white flour while retaining the most valuable parts of the wheat grain.”

The biggest difference between pizza dough and focaccia di Recco dough, Capece says, is that the latter contains no yeast. “It is made to be stretched extremely thin, while remaining elastic and strong enough to hold the cheese filling.”

And the cheese? Many bakers are steadfast in saying that only crescenza should be used. “We use only carefully selected crescenza cheese with a low fat content, otherwise, the cheese would melt too much during baking and would not give the desired result,” explains Revello.

Focaccia di Recco is typically baked in a pan, and this is where the true skill of a baker shines. “The dough must be stretched into an extremely thin sheet, almost transparent, and only experienced hands can achieve that consistency,” says Revello. “You should almost be able to see through the top layer before baking. This is one of the defining characteristics of an authentic focaccia di Recco.”

Baking the bread in a pizza oven is ideal. “Both pizza and focaccia di Recco require very high temperatures, but the goals are different,” says Capece. “Pizza needs a balanced heat from both the bottom and the top to develop a crisp base and a well-cooked crust. Focaccia di Recco also needs intense heat, but especially from above, to quickly brown the thin dough while keeping the cheese creamy.”

Revello adds that the main limitation of a home oven is its maximum temperature. “At lower temperatures, the focaccia needs to bake for longer, which tends to dry out the dough rather than keeping it light and delicate,” he says.

“Every focacciaio has a unique touch,” says Bernini. “That is why we invite all our guests to try various bakeries or restaurants of our consortium.”

Revello has tried many versions of focaccia di Recco, but, in his opinion, nothing beats “sitting on the beach, eating it with your hands while looking out at the sea in Camogli.”

Revello Camogli’s Focaccia di Recco Recipe

Ingredients

4 cups (500 grams) Type 0 flour (may substitute bread flour)

¼ cup (50 grams) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for the pan

1 cup (about 240 grams) water

1 teaspoon fine salt

Approximately 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram) of fresh crescenza (stracchino) cheese

Directions

To make the dough, mix the flour, oil, water and salt until well combined. Let the dough rest for about 30 minutes.

If you have a pizza oven, preheat it to 570°F. Otherwise, preheat a home oven to its maximum heat, about 500°F.

Divide the dough into two pieces, one about two-thirds of the total. Place the larger piece on a well-oiled pizza pan and stretch to cover the pan. Drop dots of cheese all over the dough. Roll or hand-stretch the smaller piece of dough as thinly as possible. Lay this thin sheet on top of the cheese. Prick large holes in the dough to let out any trapped air.

Bake the focaccia for 7 to 8 minutes, or longer if you’re baking at a lower heat. It is ready when the top is golden and the bottom slides freely on the baking pan. Slice and serve while hot.

blocks.x: A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It’s Addictive
Unlike the pillowy-soft focaccia that’s more widely known, focaccia di Recco is thin, crispy and filled with gooey cheese

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/2Ht5uDMp7uS_kh4NdYKp4LgDvYs=/1026x684/filters:focal(1061x707:1062x708)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/94/b5/94b559ec-2e96-4ec2-b75f-599585cefacd/gettyimages-1475006586.jpg
blocks.c: focaccia di Recco

blocks.x: This summer, I found myself on a mission. As temperatures soared into the mid-90s during Europe’s heat wave, I packed my bags and embarked on a six-hour road trip from Switzerland to Liguria. Rather than seeking out seasonal treats like granita or gelato, I was headed to the Italian coast for focaccia.

When most Americans­—and Italians, for that matter—think of focaccia, they think of the pillowy-soft version that’s leavened with yeast, baked in a sheet pan and perfect for scarpetta, or the mopping up of delicious sauces. However, ask any Ligurian, and they will tell you that the focaccia that reigns supreme is focaccia di Recco.

Focaccia di Recco is a specialty dish in Liguria. Starkly different from the carbohydrate found in the United States, this yeast-free snack is a thin flatbread filled with gooey cheese—usually crescenza or stracchino—and baked in a super-hot oven until crispy and golden brown.

Certified as just one of four foods of the Ligurian coast with a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation from the European Union, an official focaccia di Recco can be made only in Recco or neighboring Camogli, Sori or Avegno. Along with sea-salt cured anchovies, basil and olive oil, focaccia di Recco is the pride of the Ligurian people. For two decades, a consortium, the Consorzio della Focaccia di Recco, has safeguarded the legend of the bread by promoting it through annual events like the Recco Focaccia Festival.

“The focaccia di Recco celebrates authenticity, local traditions and is a connection between food, people and place,” says Giovanni Astolfoni, a Genoa native who is executive chef of Botanico Restaurant in Nervi. “It is much more than a local specialty. It perfectly reflects the spirit of Ligurian cooking. … It looks simple, yet making it well takes experience, patience and respect for the ingredients.”

Even revered pizza makers in Italy hold focaccia di Recco in high esteem, agreeing that it is worth the pilgrimage. “What impresses me most is its simplicity and the incredible craftsmanship behind it,” says Francesco Capece, owner of Confine in Milan, recently named Italy’s best pizzeria. “With just a few ingredients, it creates a perfect balance between the crispy, paper-thin dough and the creamy cheese filling. It is a beautiful example of how Italian tradition transforms simple ingredients into something extraordinary.”

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/F24Ec8E4KLTE4x6gM8Hm9MuYNXE=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1061x707:1062x708)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/09/b2/09b2daca-b1f6-4f67-ad72-f5445984d38f/gettyimages-2076422468.jpg
blocks.c: Recco Italy

blocks.x: History of Focaccia di Recco

According to the consortium, the history of focaccia di Recco can be traced back to 1189, when a version of the bread appeared on the table of medieval knights before they made their departure for the Holy Land during the Third Crusade. However, it was during the raids by Saracen pirates around the 16th century that focaccia di Recco became what it is today, confirms Lucio Bernini, the consortium’s director. Research shows that as locals from Recco fled to the mountains, the ingredients they carried with them—flour, oil and cheese—were combined and cooked over slate stone. At the end of the 1800s, bakeries and taverns sold focaccia di Recco to residents in celebration of All Souls’ Day (November 2), the day after All Saints’ Day, which marks a two-day Christian observance of saints and martyrs, as well as those who are deceased. Nowadays, focaccia di Recco is a staple in the Ligurian diet, with locals in the region’s four provinces having constant access to it throughout the day.
Did you know? The earliest focaccia
Neolithic communities in the Middle East were baking focaccia-like flatbreads between 7000 and 5000 B.C.E., according a 2024 study in Scientific Reports.

In the 19th century, Panificio Moltedo, a bakery that still stands in Recco, was the first to sell focaccia di Recco. The now fifth-generation-owned bakery recently celebrated its 150th year making its wafer-thin pastry; unlike other bakeries and taverns, Panificio Moltedo does not bake its focaccia in a pan but rather directly on the deck of the oven, like a pizza, for maximum crispness. Another longtime favorite is Manuelina. The restaurant’s namesake ran a tavern outside of Recco in the late 1800s and is credited with making focaccia di Recco mainstream by serving it every day. Her descendants opened a simple focacceria in town in 1983 to keep up with demand. “Manuelina took the popular recipe and was the first to start selling it every day and for everyone to enjoy, But they did not invent focaccia di Recco,” says Bernini.

In the past century and a half, a handful of other eateries have opened along the Italian Riviera selling focaccia di Recco. One of those is Revello Camogli in the resort town of Camogli. “We have been making focaccia di Recco ever since my grandfather took over the business in 1964,” says third-generation owner Umberto Revello. “Running a bakery like ours requires a great deal of time, so the bakery becomes a second home—if not the first. Since we were children, we have grown up watching our father and grandfather make focaccia every day. It naturally became part of our family tradition.” He says that it’s more than a family business; focaccia represents an important part of his identity.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/k76zo0eHJpoLSlVRr60EmIQ0-78=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(512x341:513x342)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/17/81/178181e4-d0ae-4925-bf85-5359eada25f2/gettyimages-1314659361.jpg
blocks.c: foccacia di Recco at Moltedo bakery

blocks.x: Second-generation focaccia di Recco maker Fabrizio Passano agrees. “My father, Alfredo, started making focaccia di Recco in 1967, and for the last 59 years, we have continued the tradition,” says the chef at Alfredo Ristorante in Recco. “Focaccia di Recco is a symbol of an ancient tradition we hold incredibly dear.”

Once I arrived in Recco, the focaccia, advertised on blackboard menus and in bakeries around town, was hard to miss. The blisters that formed on the roof of my mouth as I sampled different vendors’ versions of the bread filled with piping hot cheese were well worth it.

“While every restaurant has their own differences in technique, there really is only one recipe,” says Passano, acknowledging the focaccia’s PGI status. “So you have to stick with the plan.” When I stop into Alfredo Ristorante, the chef tosses the focaccia dough in the air with very little effort. Clearly, he has made many, and the result is a very thin and crispy focaccia. The cheese is chewy and makes a squeaking noise when I bite into it.

Over lunch at Alfredo, Bernini tells me the consortium consists of 12 members with 19 destinations, including bakeries, take-away eateries and restaurants spread across the Ligurian coast. “The PGI preserves the true history and tradition against increasingly widespread imitations,” the former hotelier adds.

According to Bernini, without the PGI stamp, the focaccia should not be called focaccia di Recco and should bear the name focaccia col formaggio (focaccia with cheese). A handful of restaurants in the United States, including Chi Spacca in Los Angeles, Rosie Cannonball in Houston and Keste in New York City, have the specialty on their menus.
How to make focaccia di Recco

According to Bernini, Passano and Revello, achieving a perfect focaccia di Recco comes down to the skills of the focacciai (a Ligurian term for focaccia makers). But all three agree that you can make the bread at home with a few simple tips.

“An important element to making a great focaccia di Recco is using high-quality ingredients,” says Revello. He continues, “Firstly, the flour. We use a strong Italian Type ‘0’ flour, which has an appearance of traditional white flour while retaining the most valuable parts of the wheat grain.”
https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/kiCDHCV08PtZ4CVonya7ng3cvh8=/fit-in/200x200/filters:no_upscale()/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/headshot/Michelle_Tchea-edit.png
blocks.c: Michelle Tchea

blocks.x: The biggest difference between pizza dough and focaccia di Recco dough, Capece says, is that the latter contains no yeast. “It is made to be stretched extremely thin, while remaining elastic and strong enough to hold the cheese filling.”

And the cheese? Many bakers are steadfast in saying that only crescenza should be used. “We use only carefully selected crescenza cheese with a low fat content, otherwise, the cheese would melt too much during baking and would not give the desired result,” explains Revello.

Focaccia di Recco is typically baked in a pan, and this is where the true skill of a baker shines. “The dough must be stretched into an extremely thin sheet, almost transparent, and only experienced hands can achieve that consistency,” says Revello. “You should almost be able to see through the top layer before baking. This is one of the defining characteristics of an authentic focaccia di Recco.”

Baking the bread in a pizza oven is ideal. “Both pizza and focaccia di Recco require very high temperatures, but the goals are different,” says Capece. “Pizza needs a balanced heat from both the bottom and the top to develop a crisp base and a well-cooked crust. Focaccia di Recco also needs intense heat, but especially from above, to quickly brown the thin dough while keeping the cheese creamy.”

Revello adds that the main limitation of a home oven is its maximum temperature. “At lower temperatures, the focaccia needs to bake for longer, which tends to dry out the dough rather than keeping it light and delicate,” he says.
“Every focacciaio has a unique touch,” says Bernini. “That is why we invite all our guests to try various bakeries or restaurants of our consortium.”
Revello has tried many versions of focaccia di Recco, but, in his opinion, nothing beats “sitting on the beach, eating it with your hands while looking out at the sea in Camogli.”

4 cups (500 grams) Type 0 flour (may substitute bread flour)
¼ cup (50 grams) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for the pan
1 cup (about 240 grams) water
1 teaspoon fine salt
Approximately 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram) of fresh crescenza (stracchino) cheese
Directions
To make the dough, mix the flour, oil, water and salt until well combined. Let the dough rest for about 30 minutes.
If you have a pizza oven, preheat it to 570°F. Otherwise, preheat a home oven to its maximum heat, about 500°F.

Divide the dough into two pieces, one about two-thirds of the total. Place the larger piece on a well-oiled pizza pan and stretch to cover the pan. Drop dots of cheese all over the dough. Roll or hand-stretch the smaller piece of dough as thinly as possible. Lay this thin sheet on top of the cheese. Prick large holes in the dough to let out any trapped air.
Bake the focaccia for 7 to 8 minutes, or longer if you’re baking at a lower heat. It is ready when the top is golden and the bottom slides freely on the baking pan. Slice and serve while hot.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.

items.title: The Ultimate Gift Guide for Home Cooks
items.summary: When it comes to finding gifts for people who love to cook, I stand by a simple gift shopping mantra: Know what your giftee likes, and then expand upon (or
items.text:
When it comes to finding gifts for people who love to cook, I stand by a simple gift shopping mantra: Know what your giftee likes, and then expand upon (or improve) their area of interest. Meaning, if they’re always tracking down rare spices, gift them a pirate’s hoard of blends from one of our favorite places to buy spices online; if they love to bake, equip them with a charming set of nontoxic, miniature muffin baking pans. And so on and so forth; basically, pay attention to what needs an upgrade in their life (there’s a good chance it’s cooking utensils) and which knives aren’t cutting it in their rotation.

Whether you’re shopping on a budget or looking for a splurge-worthy piece of cookware or bundle of pantry staples, we’ve got the gift for you and the picky cook that you love.

A sleek Japanese santoku knife

I think of a santoku as the sexier version of a classic chef’s knife, because while it’s designed to handle meat, fish, and vegetables like a pro, a santoku blade is often a bit lighter on its feet (read: cutting board) that other styles of do-it-all knives. This particular option from Mercer Culinary is a line cook favorite.


Mercer Culinary M20707 Genesis 7-Inch Santoku Knife

Where to Buy:

$39.95 at Mercer Culinary Store


This artisan-made molcajete

If your giftee is always on the literal grind for their recipes, chances are they could use a molcajete, a traditional Mexican mortar and pestle. This large, 9-inch version was made in collaboration with the third-generation stone artisan Don Enrique of San Salvador El Seco, Puebla, and includes a particularly cool, graphic tejolote (grinding pestle).


Masienda Molcajete

Where to Buy:

$95 at Masienda


Fancy tinned tomatoes

Row 7 has made quite a stir in the food world this year. Founded in 2018, the organic seed and food company is the brainchild of chef Dan Barber, plant breeder Michael Mazourek, and seedsman Matthew Goldfarb, and was initially focused on collaborating with farmers on a smaller scale in order to produce more flavor-focused (as opposed to maximum output-focused) produce. This last winter, folks yielded the fruits of their labor; a line of complex, flavor-packed tinned veggies was launched, including my personal favorite, the tinned tomatoes. They’re bright, jammy, and an absolute indulgence. Just what gifts are for.


Row 7 Sweet Prince Tomato Tins (3 Pack)

Where to Buy:

$29 at Row 7


This hand cream dethrones Aesop

If you love someone who loves to cook, their hands could probably use some love, too. Monastery’s everything balm (I use it on my hands and dry legs) feels like the love child of Aesop and Aquaphor, because it’s equal parts unisex, herbaceous remedy and non-fuss, non-greasy (and non-overly-perfumed) clear balm. The little silver tube is also the most giftable of hand creams for my money, complete with an antique-looking tube roller key for squeezing out every last drop.


Monastery Universal Balm

Where to Buy:

$48 at Monastery


The more cool Finnish dish towels, the merrier

Finnish design house Marimekko is one of Eater staffers’ absolute favorite brands for pops of color and graphic design, and this striking towel duo would make a great, seasonal-spanning addition to any cook’s kitchen.


Marimekko Unikko Organic Cotton Kitchen Towels

Where to Buy:

$52 at Amazon


Nordic Ware sheet pans

There are certainly cuter sheet pans out there, but aesthetics are a low priority when it comes to good, always-reach-for-it bakeware. Seasoned cooks and bakers know: It’s all about the straightforward functionality of Nordic Ware. Irresistibly affordable at $40 for a set of three (including a tiny quarter-sheet that’s great for organizing mise en place and baking just a cookie or two from the freezer), these sheet pans bake evenly and resist rust and warping. Best of all, they last, unlike all the wonky nonstick sheet pans we’ve put up with in the past.


Naturals 3 Piece Baker’s Delight Set

Where to Buy:

$40 $36.9 at Amazon

$40 at Nordic Ware


This cottagecore apron is doing so many things right

This, folks, is what happens when you create a charming apron with substance. The midweight cotton material checks the box for durability, while avoiding the stiffness that sometimes comes with other self-declared tough aprons. There are two extra large pockets for all of your tools, and, perhaps my favorite feature of all, a cross-back design, so you don’t have to worry about re-tying and adjusting your apron strings.


Big Night Gingham Smock Apron

Where to Buy:

$55 at Big Night


Do they love spicy food? Stock their pantry with high-quality staples

Flamingo Estate has earned its place in the olive oil hall of fame for its Martha Stewart-approved heritage olive oil, and it recently started infusing its liquid gold with guajillo chiles to add a bit of fruity heat to the versatile, peppery olive oil. The spicy heritage EVOO is also sold with its smoked chipotle chile crisp as part of a very giftable duo.


Flamingo Estate Spicy Finishing Set

Where to Buy:

$108 at Flamingo Estate


Versatile glassware

Bustling home kitchens often beget broken glassware. As someone who loves to host, I keep a cabinet of tall tumblers stocked for birthday parties, barbecues, and dinners and brunches at home. This robust set of 14-ounce crystal tumblers from the Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa collaboration can handsomely serve everything from juice to batch cocktails.


Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Modus Crystal 14-oz Glass (Set of 8)

Where to Buy:

$47.95 at Amazon


A supply of beans

Beans, like all pantry staples, have gotten upgrade in recent years. Primary Beans is a company that promotes lesser-known bean varieties (see their not-a-pinto set). If you’ve ever been skeptical of whether fresher beans really matter, these flavorful beans — which cite their harvest dates with pride — will remove any doubt. They’ll make an especially good gift for a cook looking to diversify their protein sources.


Primary Beans “All the Beans” Set

Where to Buy:

$144.86 at Primary Beans


Spices you can’t find at every grocery store

There’s an entire Eater guide to shopping for spices online, but some of my favorite picks come from Shop Palestine and Hayati; the former is a project of the Middle East Children’s Alliance, a nonprofit working to support the rights and the wellbeing of children in Gaza by amplifying products from the region, such as this za’atar, harvested from the hills of Palestine. Hayati, meanwhile, is a newcomer to the spice scene that was founded by Palestinian-American Yasmine Borno with the goal of highlighting distinctly Palestinian flavors; she sources Hayati’s za’atar ingredients from the same spice shop in Palestine that was beloved by her own great-grandparents.


Shop Palestine Baladna Za’atar (12 oz)

Where to Buy:

$12 at Shop Palestine

Hayati Green Za’atar

Where to Buy:

$11.99 at Hayati


The Bentley of cutting boards

I have yet to find a cutting board that can outdo a John Boos in matters of durability and function; the sustainably sourced maple, cherry, and walnut boards have been made by the same Midwest-based company since 1887, and while its fine craftsmanship can easily boost the boards’ price tags to $100+, there are some beautiful, more affordable options out there, such as this limited-counter-space-friendly, 1-inch thick, square format cutting board.


John Boos Cutting Board (12”x12”)

Where to Buy:

$59.95 at Amazon


Six months of pasta

Whether it’s bougie hand soap, merino wool socks, or artisanal pasta, high-end everyday items are always a good gift, especially for someone who doesn’t tend to treat themselves. Sfoglini’s bronze-cut pasta, made from a range of grains including einkorn and rye, is extruded through bronze dies into a variety of specialty shapes before being slow-dried. The result is a slightly rougher (and overall better) texture that holds its shape. This subscription includes two shipments of six boxes of pasta — some for now, some for later.


Sfoglini

Where to Buy:

$110 at Sfoglini


A bread chopping board

What do you get the cook who has everything? That’s when you start troubleshooting hyperspecific culinary problems you imagine they’re having. So, save a bread lover from the constant tyranny of crumbs with this handy slotted cutting board. Its many wide divots will catch the shards from their crustiest baguettes, and every errant seed from their most-flecked loaves. You just solved a problem they didn’t realize needed solving.


Dyke & Dean Chopping Board

Where to Buy:

$25 at Dyke & Dean


Miniature muffin pans for the avid baker

Making muffins can be so satisfying under any circumstances, but The Borrowers-size cinnamon nut muffins in a trio of light pink miniature muffin pans? The dream.


Caraway Mini Muffin Pan Trio

Where to Buy:

$125 at Caraway


This Funfetti-esque spatula set

Admittedly, I still have a few scratched-up plastic spatulas floating around my kitchen. But given the potential health risks of black plastic utensils, there has never been a better time to help swap out your gifted culinary pal’s tools with Get It Right’s nontoxic, microplastic-free silicone cooking accessories. This speckled, Funfetti-esque spatula set looks good enough to eat.


Get It Right 3-Piece Sprinkles Spatula Set

Where to Buy:

$34.95 at Get It Right


Soaps for home cooks are officially chic now

I’m a big fan of fancy hand soaps — just one of life’s everyday sensory luxuries — and recently, the concept of swish soaps specifically designed to live at the kitchen sink have been catching my eye; Naomi makes a lightly exfoliating, bergamot and pepper hand soap that is formulated to banish the garlic odor from your fingertips while also looking quite chic by your sink.


Naomi After-Cooking Hand Scrub (Bergamot & Pepper)

Where to Buy:

$29 $27 at Amazon


A magnetic wood trivet

In her debut cookbook The Secret of Cooking, Bee Wilson gives more credit than most to the humble trivet: “Without them [in addition to discard bowls, she writes], the whole business of cooking is so much trickier than it needs to be.” While a basic trivet does the job, consider giving the gift of a magnetic trivet. Skip the awkward maneuvering of carrying a hot, heavy dish to the dining table and use a trivet that attaches itself to the bottom of the pot instead. This one is designed for a Staub Dutch oven, but Le Creuset makes one as well.


Staub Magnetic Wood Trivet (9-inch)

Where to Buy:

$44.99 at Zwilling


A pair of squeeze bottles

Home cooks are increasingly adopting what chefs have long known — that squeeze bottles give you the most control over your oils, vinegars, and sauces while cooking, not to mention the perfect drizzles and drops while plating. (At this point, we’re all well aware of that social media-famous squeeze bottle of olive oil.) OXO’s squeeze bottles, which come in two sizes, have attached hinged caps for easy one-handed use.


OXO 6-oz Squeeze Bottles (3 Pack)

Where to Buy:

$11.19 at Walmart


A frying pan that can handle four chicken breasts

Ah, the peace of knowing that all four of my desired chicken breasts would fit, uncrowded, in this sleek pan for chicken picatta night. As lovers of quality cookware, Eater collaborated with Heritage Steel on a collection of 5-ply stainless steel pots and pans, and the line includes this much-welcome, do-it-all, 12-inch lidded skillet.


Eater x Heritage Steel Fry Pan With Lid (12-inch)

Where to Buy:

$149.95 at Heritage Steel


Soup season is almost here

Another stand out of the Eater x Heritage Steel collection is this 8-quart stock pot, which has carried me through many a soup season. The 5-ply stainless steel is incredibly durable, yet lightweight enough that I can still carry it when it’s full of ungodly amounts of chili.


Eater x Heritage Steel 8 Quart Stock Pot with Lid

Where to Buy:

$229.95 at Heritage Steel


Gold tweezers

Tweezers often end up at the butt end of jokes about fussy food. But there’s no denying they’re useful in the kitchen doing what tongs can, but, in many instances, better. Tongs can break off the delicate breading on a cutlet, while tweezers press gently, leaving it undisturbed. They’re dextrous enough to maneuver tiny herb garnishes or decorations on top of a cake. And these, from fancy Japanese kitchen tool company Gestura, just look really, really good, whether you get them in gold, silver, or gunmetal.


Gestura Gold Tweezers

Where to Buy:

$37 at Carbon Knife Co.


A spare grinder for nuts and coffee

I’ve experienced the gamut of grinders, and tend to look for a few green flags: an ample “grinding” chamber, a simple design, and a trusted brand. This KitchenAid iteration checks all three of those boxes, and it even comes in the brand’s iconic Empire Red colorway.


KitchenAid Blade Coffee Grinder (4 oz)

Where to Buy:

$49.99 $44.99 at Amazon

$49.95 at Webstaurantstore


A sunny grill press

It’s debatable how beneficial pressure is in many parts of life. But when it comes to ensuring the most even cooking, pressure will give you uniformly golden grilled cheeses, pan-fried fish with perfectly browned skin, and beautifully seared mushrooms. This marigold press from Caraway is the most visually charming for my money, and the slightly curved handle makes it much easier to hold.


Caraway Marigold Grill Press

Where to Buy:

$85 at Caraway


A pasta machine

Get this for the friend who keeps saying, Going out to dinner — in this economy? Fresh pasta is relatively affordable, but maybe more importantly, the act of making it will scratch that experiential, interactive itch that might otherwise be fulfilled by a night out. Feeling extra generous? Pair this no-frills pasta machine with a cookbook like American Sfoglino: A Master Class in Handmade Pasta, from Los Angeles pasta icon Evan Funke.


Marcato Atlas 150 Pasta Machine

Where to Buy:

$154.95 at Crate and Barrel

The more cool Finnish dish towels, the merrier

Finnish design house Marimekko is one of Eater staffers’ absolute favorite brands for pops of color and graphic design, and this striking towel duo would make a great, seasonal-spanning addition to any cook’s kitchen.
Marimekko Unikko Organic Cotton Kitchen Towels
Where to Buy:
$52 at Amazon
Nordic Ware sheet pans

There are certainly cuter sheet pans out there, but aesthetics are a low priority when it comes to good, always-reach-for-it bakeware. Seasoned cooks and bakers know: It’s all about the straightforward functionality of Nordic Ware. Irresistibly affordable at $40 for a set of three (including a tiny quarter-sheet that’s great for organizing mise en place and baking just a cookie or two from the freezer), these sheet pans bake evenly and resist rust and warping. Best of all, they last, unlike all the wonky nonstick sheet pans we’ve put up with in the past.
Naturals 3 Piece Baker’s Delight Set
Where to Buy:
$40 $36.9 at Amazon
$40 at Nordic Ware
This cottagecore apron is doing so many things right

This, folks, is what happens when you create a charming apron with substance. The midweight cotton material checks the box for durability, while avoiding the stiffness that sometimes comes with other self-declared tough aprons. There are two extra large pockets for all of your tools, and, perhaps my favorite feature of all, a cross-back design, so you don’t have to worry about re-tying and adjusting your apron strings.
Big Night Gingham Smock Apron
Where to Buy:
$55 at Big Night
Do they love spicy food? Stock their pantry with high-quality staples

Flamingo Estate has earned its place in the olive oil hall of fame for its Martha Stewart-approved heritage olive oil, and it recently started infusing its liquid gold with guajillo chiles to add a bit of fruity heat to the versatile, peppery olive oil. The spicy heritage EVOO is also sold with its smoked chipotle chile crisp as part of a very giftable duo.
Flamingo Estate Spicy Finishing Set
Where to Buy:
$108 at Flamingo Estate
Versatile glassware

Bustling home kitchens often beget broken glassware. As someone who loves to host, I keep a cabinet of tall tumblers stocked for birthday parties, barbecues, and dinners and brunches at home. This robust set of 14-ounce crystal tumblers from the Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa collaboration can handsomely serve everything from juice to batch cocktails.
Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Modus Crystal 14-oz Glass (Set of 8)
Where to Buy:
$47.95 at Amazon
A supply of beans

Beans, like all pantry staples, have gotten upgrade in recent years. Primary Beans is a company that promotes lesser-known bean varieties (see their not-a-pinto set). If you’ve ever been skeptical of whether fresher beans really matter, these flavorful beans — which cite their harvest dates with pride — will remove any doubt. They’ll make an especially good gift for a cook looking to diversify their protein sources.
Primary Beans “All the Beans” Set
Where to Buy:
$144.86 at Primary Beans
Spices you can’t find at every grocery store

There’s an entire Eater guide to shopping for spices online, but some of my favorite picks come from Shop Palestine and Hayati; the former is a project of the Middle East Children’s Alliance, a nonprofit working to support the rights and the wellbeing of children in Gaza by amplifying products from the region, such as this za’atar, harvested from the hills of Palestine. Hayati, meanwhile, is a newcomer to the spice scene that was founded by Palestinian-American Yasmine Borno with the goal of highlighting distinctly Palestinian flavors; she sources Hayati’s za’atar ingredients from the same spice shop in Palestine that was beloved by her own great-grandparents.
Shop Palestine Baladna Za’atar (12 oz)
Where to Buy:
$12 at Shop Palestine
Hayati Green Za’atar
Where to Buy:
$11.99 at Hayati
The Bentley of cutting boards

I have yet to find a cutting board that can outdo a John Boos in matters of durability and function; the sustainably sourced maple, cherry, and walnut boards have been made by the same Midwest-based company since 1887, and while its fine craftsmanship can easily boost the boards’ price tags to $100+, there are some beautiful, more affordable options out there, such as this limited-counter-space-friendly, 1-inch thick, square format cutting board.
John Boos Cutting Board (12”x12”)
Where to Buy:
$59.95 at Amazon
Six months of pasta

Whether it’s bougie hand soap, merino wool socks, or artisanal pasta, high-end everyday items are always a good gift, especially for someone who doesn’t tend to treat themselves. Sfoglini’s bronze-cut pasta, made from a range of grains including einkorn and rye, is extruded through bronze dies into a variety of specialty shapes before being slow-dried. The result is a slightly rougher (and overall better) texture that holds its shape. This subscription includes two shipments of six boxes of pasta — some for now, some for later.
Sfoglini
Where to Buy:
$110 at Sfoglini
A bread chopping board

What do you get the cook who has everything? That’s when you start troubleshooting hyperspecific culinary problems you imagine they’re having. So, save a bread lover from the constant tyranny of crumbs with this handy slotted cutting board. Its many wide divots will catch the shards from their crustiest baguettes, and every errant seed from their most-flecked loaves. You just solved a problem they didn’t realize needed solving.
Dyke & Dean Chopping Board
Where to Buy:
$25 at Dyke & Dean
Miniature muffin pans for the avid baker
Making muffins can be so satisfying under any circumstances, but The Borrowers-size cinnamon nut muffins in a trio of light pink miniature muffin pans? The dream.
Caraway Mini Muffin Pan Trio
Where to Buy:
$125 at Caraway
This Funfetti-esque spatula set

Admittedly, I still have a few scratched-up plastic spatulas floating around my kitchen. But given the potential health risks of black plastic utensils, there has never been a better time to help swap out your gifted culinary pal’s tools with Get It Right’s nontoxic, microplastic-free silicone cooking accessories. This speckled, Funfetti-esque spatula set looks good enough to eat.
Get It Right 3-Piece Sprinkles Spatula Set
Where to Buy:
$34.95 at Get It Right
Soaps for home cooks are officially chic now

I’m a big fan of fancy hand soaps — just one of life’s everyday sensory luxuries — and recently, the concept of swish soaps specifically designed to live at the kitchen sink have been catching my eye; Naomi makes a lightly exfoliating, bergamot and pepper hand soap that is formulated to banish the garlic odor from your fingertips while also looking quite chic by your sink.
Naomi After-Cooking Hand Scrub (Bergamot & Pepper)
Where to Buy:
$29 $27 at Amazon
A magnetic wood trivet

In her debut cookbook The Secret of Cooking, Bee Wilson gives more credit than most to the humble trivet: “Without them [in addition to discard bowls, she writes], the whole business of cooking is so much trickier than it needs to be.” While a basic trivet does the job, consider giving the gift of a magnetic trivet. Skip the awkward maneuvering of carrying a hot, heavy dish to the dining table and use a trivet that attaches itself to the bottom of the pot instead. This one is designed for a Staub Dutch oven, but Le Creuset makes one as well.
Staub Magnetic Wood Trivet (9-inch)
Where to Buy:
$44.99 at Zwilling
A pair of squeeze bottles

Home cooks are increasingly adopting what chefs have long known — that squeeze bottles give you the most control over your oils, vinegars, and sauces while cooking, not to mention the perfect drizzles and drops while plating. (At this point, we’re all well aware of that social media-famous squeeze bottle of olive oil.) OXO’s squeeze bottles, which come in two sizes, have attached hinged caps for easy one-handed use.
OXO 6-oz Squeeze Bottles (3 Pack)
Where to Buy:
$11.19 at Walmart
A frying pan that can handle four chicken breasts

Ah, the peace of knowing that all four of my desired chicken breasts would fit, uncrowded, in this sleek pan for chicken picatta night. As lovers of quality cookware, Eater collaborated with Heritage Steel on a collection of 5-ply stainless steel pots and pans, and the line includes this much-welcome, do-it-all, 12-inch lidded skillet.
Eater x Heritage Steel Fry Pan With Lid (12-inch)
Where to Buy:
$149.95 at Heritage Steel
Soup season is almost here

Another stand out of the Eater x Heritage Steel collection is this 8-quart stock pot, which has carried me through many a soup season. The 5-ply stainless steel is incredibly durable, yet lightweight enough that I can still carry it when it’s full of ungodly amounts of chili.
Eater x Heritage Steel 8 Quart Stock Pot with Lid
Where to Buy:
$229.95 at Heritage Steel
Gold tweezers

Tweezers often end up at the butt end of jokes about fussy food. But there’s no denying they’re useful in the kitchen doing what tongs can, but, in many instances, better. Tongs can break off the delicate breading on a cutlet, while tweezers press gently, leaving it undisturbed. They’re dextrous enough to maneuver tiny herb garnishes or decorations on top of a cake. And these, from fancy Japanese kitchen tool company Gestura, just look really, really good, whether you get them in gold, silver, or gunmetal.
Gestura Gold Tweezers
Where to Buy:
$37 at Carbon Knife Co.
A spare grinder for nuts and coffee

I’ve experienced the gamut of grinders, and tend to look for a few green flags: an ample “grinding” chamber, a simple design, and a trusted brand. This KitchenAid iteration checks all three of those boxes, and it even comes in the brand’s iconic Empire Red colorway.
KitchenAid Blade Coffee Grinder (4 oz)
Where to Buy:
$49.99 $44.99 at Amazon
$49.95 at Webstaurantstore
A sunny grill press

It’s debatable how beneficial pressure is in many parts of life. But when it comes to ensuring the most even cooking, pressure will give you uniformly golden grilled cheeses, pan-fried fish with perfectly browned skin, and beautifully seared mushrooms. This marigold press from Caraway is the most visually charming for my money, and the slightly curved handle makes it much easier to hold.
Caraway Marigold Grill Press
Where to Buy:
$85 at Caraway
A pasta machine

Get this for the friend who keeps saying, Going out to dinner — in this economy? Fresh pasta is relatively affordable, but maybe more importantly, the act of making it will scratch that experiential, interactive itch that might otherwise be fulfilled by a night out. Feeling extra generous? Pair this no-frills pasta machine with a cookbook like American Sfoglino: A Master Class in Handmade Pasta, from Los Angeles pasta icon Evan Funke.
Marcato Atlas 150 Pasta Machine
Where to Buy:
$154.95 at Crate and Barrel

items.title: Are AI-Made Reservations Fair?
items.author: Sam Stone
items.summary: Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop
items.text:
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop Date.’

Welcome back to Open Tab. Labor Day weekend was excuse enough for me to make salmon tacos with pineapple-chile salsa—always a hit—followed by a fluffy, aromatic olive oil cake. I’ve found myself cooking at home almost exclusively in recent weeks, but, in no particular order, here are the New York Restaurants I’ve been meaning to hit: Dean’s, Hommali, Kirbee’s, Graciela, and El Califa de Leon. Make of that list what you will.

This week marks 25 years since the attacks on 9/11—many in the food world are remembering Windows on the World, the restaurant opened on the top floors of the North Tower. CNN also released a documentary on the restaurant, which was at one time the highest-grossing standalone restaurant in the country.

Another fascinating read: Ruby Tandoh in the New Yorker on Saudi Arabia’s quest to rebrand as a culinary capital which includes, among other things, the introduction of Michelin stars last year. Michelin has been evaluating more and more cities, often partnering with (read: getting paid by) local tourism boards who recognize that the distinction can attract a real wave of tourists to the area. But when I interviewed him a couple years ago, Gwendal Poullennec, international director of the Michelin Guide, insisted that the guide’s expansion wasn’t about the money—it was about finding more cities with “culinary potential” than ever before.

Oh, also they’re doing $60 loaves of rye bread now. Oy.

Also in this week’s Open Tab: the people using AI agents to score reservations, what exactly are ultraprocessed foods?, and the eternal question: Is it ever ok to bring your own seasonings to restaurants?

AI agents? I have reservations

This week’s addition to the AI hellscape? Personal AI agents. Meta released Muse, and Instinct continues to gain traction. These are agents that can respond to emails, book plane tickets, secure you a spot in a workout class, arrange and rearrange your calendar, and, yes, make grab that impossible-to-get dinner reservation. Hypothetically.

Using AI agents to nab tough reservations may also get you banned from reservation platforms, as one user found out this week. The way these agents work is by spamming the reservation platform hundreds of times per hour for hours on end. The reservation platforms flag that as suspicious activity, and may ban your account.

When I reached out to Resy for comment, a spokesperson clarified that the company doesn’t permit “unapproved third-party bots or AI agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform.” That’s not to say the company is anti-AI—it’s recently announced integrations with ChatGPT and Claude. But rather, it says, Resy wants to maintain a “fair reservation experience for diners.”

And that’s really the crux of the issue; it’s not hard to imagine a day in the not-too-distant future when AI agents can work within a platform's terms of service (in fact, that day may have actually been earlier this week) grabbing the toughest tables the second they become available. It’s an undeniable upping of the ante in the already impossible reservations war. What are non-agent-assisted restaurant lovers to do? How can restaurants, many dependent on these platforms to stay booked, respond? Is this the beginning of a golden age for walk-in only spots?

What exactly makes a food ultraprocessed?

This week, California approved a landmark bill that establishes a process for which foods may label themselves as non-ultraprocessed. This comes after the state was the first in the nation to put forth a solid definition of what exactly an ultraprocessed food is. Although there’s been a lot of talk about ultraprocessed foods (or UPFs)—mostly stemming from the MAHA movement—there’s not a true consensus on how to delineate which foods are ultraprocessed and which aren’t.

I mean, sure, maybe you simply know it when you see it: an apple is not ultraprocessed. Gently glowing, fire-engine red flamin’ hot cheetos boxed mac and cheese is ultraprocessed.

At the federal level, the US is still in the process of drawing up an official definition, but around the world, several definitions are held as true. Brazilian researchers define UPFs as all foods with industrial ingredients like sweeteners or emulsifiers. Research group Healthy Eating Research says they’re foods “processed to the extent that they are no longer recognizable as their original plant/animal source.”

Though there isn’t a firm categorization (yet), we’re already beginning to see colossal food companies respond to the discourse. PepsiCo is reportedly shifting focus to fresh foods instead of processed ones, and some cereal companies have stopped using artificial dyes. All good stuff, but I will say this: You can pry my flamin’ hot cheetos mac and cheese out of my cold, dead, cholesterol-clogged hands.

Some people bring their own birthday cakes to restaurants. Others bring their own bottle of wine to enjoy with dinner. And then there are the people who bring their own seasonings to restaurants. It’s a controversial topic, but for those who don’t leave the house without their pocket Maldon, their Calabrian chili oil, their fancy olive oil it’s really no question at all. Read Maggie Hennessy’s intriguing piece on Bon Appétit for more.

items.title: Must-Try Spots For Noodle Lovers
items.author: Holyn Thigpen

items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.
